title: Financially Illiterate
author: mutallyassuredinstruction
summary: An Australian economics teacher examines the failure of the Australian curriculum to produce financially literate graduates, using the Victorian Curriculum's vague and largely aspirational economics standards as a case study. The piece documents specific examples of curriculum language so general that it provides no meaningful guidance for instruction and notes that this vagueness is not accidental -- it reflects a political compromise between those who want personal finance education and those who want economic theory, resulting in standards that technically include both and teach neither. The author argues that financial literacy is not a 'soft skill' add-on but a genuine knowledge domain with specific conceptual content (compound interest, inflation, tax structures, investment risk) that requires systematic, sequenced instruction -- not a few standalone lessons about budgeting. The piece closes with a specific curriculum proposal: four years of economics instruction, mandatory, built around the specific conceptual content that a financially capable adult actually needs.
points: * The Victorian Curriculum's economics standards are so vague that they provide no meaningful instructional guidance -- a product of political compromise between competing curriculum factions that produces language too general to teach. * Financial literacy is a genuine knowledge domain with specific conceptual content (compound interest, tax structures, inflation, investment risk) that requires systematic, sequenced instruction -- not a few standalone budgeting lessons. * The vagueness of Australian curriculum standards in economics is not unique: most developed-world curricula have similar gaps, reflecting the same political dynamic -- everyone agrees financial literacy matters and no one agrees on what it means. * The specific conceptual knowledge adults need for financial capability (how compound interest builds wealth, how tax structures create incentives, how inflation erodes savings) is well-defined and teachable; the problem is instructional, not definitional. * The author's four-year mandatory economics proposal targets the specific gap: not economic theory for economists, not personal finance anecdotes for consumer education, but the conceptual knowledge a financially capable citizen actually needs to navigate real decisions.
quotes: The Victorian Curriculum says students should 'understand the role of financial markets in allocating resources.' What does that mean for a Year 10 lesson on Tuesday? What does the teacher teach? What does the student learn? What question appears on the test? The standard answers none of these questions, and that is not an accident.

Financial literacy is not a soft skill. It is a knowledge domain. Compound interest is not a value. It is a mathematical relationship with specific properties that determine whether you get rich or stay poor over a lifetime of financial decisions. That relationship can be taught. It can be assessed. We simply choose not to.

The student who graduates from twelve years of Australian schooling without understanding how compound interest works, what inflation does to savings, how tax brackets function, or what distinguishes equity from debt -- that student has been failed by the curriculum. The failure is not their ignorance. The failure is ours.

The political compromise that produces curriculum vagueness is well-intentioned on all sides. The personal-finance advocates want students to make better individual decisions. The economics educators want students to understand markets. The result of their compromise is standards that technically satisfy both camps and practically teach neither.

Four years of mandatory economics instruction -- not economic theory, not consumer education, but the specific conceptual knowledge a financially capable adult needs -- would not solve every problem. It would solve this one. And this one is solvable. We have just chosen not to solve it.
